name: Anker 737 Power Bank (PowerCore 24K)
description: A 24,000mAh (86.4Wh) power bank with 140W USB-C and a live display; the one bank to keep for outages if you need to charge a laptop as well as phones.
quick: 24,000mAh (86.4Wh), 140W USB-C, smart display. A 24,000mAh (86.4Wh) power bank with 140W USB-C and a live display; the one bank to keep for outages if you need to charge a laptop as well as phones.
bestFor: Charging a laptop and a family’s phones through a day-long outage
skipIf: You want a pocket bank or need an AC outlet for non-USB devices
specs: Digital display with charge level and live watts
verdict: The Anker 737 (PowerCore 24K) is the power bank to keep in the drawer for outages if you can only have one. It holds enough for a household's phones for a day or two and has the output to charge a laptop at full speed.

**What 86.4Wh buys you.** Anker rates it at 24,000mAh, or 86.4Wh, just under the 100Wh limit airlines allow without approval. A typical phone battery holds 12–19Wh, and after conversion losses of about 20%, that is roughly 3–4 full phone charges, or about one full charge for a 70Wh laptop. See [watt-hours](/glossary/watt-hours/) for how to read the numbers.

**140W is the reason to pay more.** One USB-C port delivers up to 140W, enough to charge a large laptop near full speed instead of trickling. The same port refills the bank at up to 140W, so when power flickers back on in a rolling outage, it tops up much faster than a typical bank. Two USB-C ports and one USB-A cover three devices at once.

**The display ends the guessing.** A digital screen shows remaining charge and live watts in and out, so you know whether the bank will last the night. The trade-off is weight: about 1.4 lb makes it a dense brick, not a pocket bank.

Owners praise the laptop charging and the display. The main complaint is size and weight. It is the top laptop pick in our [best portable chargers for power outages](/best-portable-chargers-for-power-outages/) roundup; the [Anker Prime 27,650mAh](/gear/anker-prime-27650-power-bank/) adds more capacity and output, and the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) is the pocket-sized partner.

Up to 140W over USB-C, enough for most laptops at full speed

No AC outlet for devices with barrel chargers

faqs.q: How many times can the Anker 737 charge an iPhone?
faqs.a: About three to four times. The bank holds 86.4Wh, and a recent iPhone battery holds roughly 12–17Wh. After about 20% conversion losses, around 69Wh reaches the phone, enough for three to four full charges depending on the model. Larger Pro Max phones land near the low end of that range.

faqs.q: Can the Anker 737 charge a laptop during a power outage?
faqs.a: Yes, most USB-C laptops. Its USB-C port delivers up to 140W, which covers nearly every USB-C laptop at full speed. With about 69Wh usable after losses, it gives roughly one full charge to a laptop with a 60–70Wh battery. Laptops that only charge through a barrel plug need a bank or station with an AC outlet.

name: Anker PowerCore 10000
description: A cheap, proven 10,000mAh (36Wh) pocket bank good for about two phone charges; buy one for each person in the house and keep them topped up for outages.
quick: 10,000mAh (36Wh), USB-A, pocket size. A cheap, proven 10,000mAh (36Wh) pocket bank good for about two phone charges; buy one for each person in the house and keep them topped up for outages.
bestFor: One pocket bank per person for phones in an outage, a glovebox or a school bag
skipIf: You need to charge a laptop or fast-charge a modern phone
specs: 1 × USB-A on the classic model; USB-C variants sold
verdict: The Anker PowerCore 10000 is the cheap, proven pocket bank to buy one of for each person in the house. It will not charge a laptop, but it keeps a phone alive for a day or two of careful use.

**What 36Wh means.** Anker rates it at 10,000mAh, about 36 [watt-hours](/glossary/watt-hours/). After roughly 20% conversion losses, that is about 29Wh usable, or two charges for a typical 12–15Wh phone battery. That is the right amount for a school bag, a glovebox or a nightstand.

**Several small banks beat one big one.** In an outage, one shared bank becomes a bottleneck, because someone is always waiting on it. At this size and price you can give everyone their own. Pair them with a larger bank like the [Anker 737](/gear/anker-737-power-bank/) for laptops, and a folding panel such as the [BigBlue 28W](/gear/bigblue-28w-solar-charger/) to refill them in daylight.

**Know which version you are buying.** The classic model has one USB-A output at 12W and charges itself over micro-USB, which is slow by current standards. Anker has sold several newer variants under similar names with USB-C, so check the listing for the ports and charging speed you want. At about 6.3 oz, the classic version weighs about as much as a phone.

Owners praise its size and reliability over years of use. The main complaint, on the classic model, is slow recharging over micro-USB. It is the pocket pick in our [best portable chargers for power outages](/best-portable-chargers-for-power-outages/) roundup.

Small and light enough for a pocket or glovebox
Inexpensive enough to buy one per person

cons: Will not charge a laptop

faqs.q: How many phone charges does the Anker PowerCore 10000 give?
faqs.a: About two for most phones. It holds 36Wh, and after roughly 20% conversion losses about 29Wh reaches the phone. A typical phone battery holds 12–15Wh, so expect two full charges, or a little less for the largest phones. With low-power mode on during an outage, that can stretch one phone across three or four days.

faqs.q: Can the Anker PowerCore 10000 charge a laptop?
faqs.a: No. The classic model’s single USB-A port delivers 12W, far below what a laptop needs, and 36Wh is small for a laptop battery anyway. For laptops, use a USB-C Power Delivery bank like the Anker 737, which delivers up to 140W, or a bank or power station with an AC outlet.

name: BigBlue 28W Solar Charger
description: A 28W folding USB solar panel with SunPower cells and three USB-A ports; the most headroom for clouds and short days when you want to fill a power bank from the sun.
quick: 28W folding USB panel, 3 USB ports, SunPower cells. A 28W folding USB solar panel with SunPower cells and three USB-A ports; the most headroom for clouds and short days when you want to fill a power bank from the sun.
bestFor: Filling a 10,000–20,000mAh power bank from the sun on hikes or in outages
skipIf: You need USB-C fast charging or want to charge a laptop
specs: Folding fabric panel with loops for hanging
28W folding USB panel, 3 USB ports, SunPower cells
verdict: The BigBlue 28W is the folding USB panel to buy when you want the most headroom for clouds, short winter days and a power bank waiting to be filled. It has more cell area than the 21W class, and that margin keeps charging going when the sun is weak.

**Expect about half the rating.** The 28W figure describes the cells under ideal lab light. After heat, angle and the 5V regulator, real output in good sun commonly lands around 12–18W. Over 5 good sun hours that is roughly 60–90Wh, enough to fill a 20,000mAh bank like the [Anker 335](/gear/anker-335-power-bank-20000mah/) (about 74Wh) on a long clear day.

**Charge a bank, not a phone.** Plug a power bank into the panel during the day, then charge phones from the bank at night. Phones stop and restart charging every time a cloud passes; a bank rides through it. Three USB-A ports let you charge a bank and a phone at once in strong sun.

**The limit is USB-A.** There is no USB-C Power Delivery, so it cannot charge a laptop or fast-charge a modern phone. For a laptop or a fridge, you need a power station and a 100W-plus panel; see the [best portable solar panel](/best-portable-solar-panel/) picks. BigBlue lists SunPower cells, and the panel folds to about book size with loops for strapping it to a pack.

Owners report it keeps a bank charging on hazy days when smaller panels stall. The main complaint is the lack of USB-C. It is the top folding pick in our [best solar power bank](/best-solar-power-bank/) roundup; compare it with the lighter [Anker PowerPort Solar 21W](/gear/anker-powerport-solar-21w/).
pros: Highest rating of the phone-sized folding panels here
SunPower cells, from a well-regarded cell maker
Three USB-A ports, so a bank and a phone can charge together

faqs.q: How long does the BigBlue 28W take to charge a phone?
faqs.a: Roughly two to four hours in strong, direct sun for a typical phone, as long as charging does not cut out. Real output usually runs 12–18W in good sun, but phones pause and restart when clouds pass. For steadier results, charge a power bank from the panel during the day and charge the phone from the bank.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the BigBlue 28W and the Anker PowerPort Solar 21W?
faqs.a: Headroom versus weight. The BigBlue has a third more panel rating and three USB-A ports, so it keeps charging better in haze and low sun. The Anker 21W is slimmer and lighter, with two USB-A ports, which suits hikers charging one phone. To fill a 20,000mAh bank daily, pick the BigBlue.

name: Anker PowerPort Solar 21W
description: A slim 21W folding USB panel with two USB-A ports and SunPower cells; the lighter, simpler choice for keeping one phone or a small power bank charged from the sun.
quick: 21W folding USB panel, 2 USB-A ports, SunPower cells. A slim 21W folding USB panel with two USB-A ports and SunPower cells; the lighter, simpler choice for keeping one phone or a small power bank charged from the sun.
bestFor: Hikers and outage kits that need to keep one phone or a small bank charged
skipIf: You want to fill a 20,000mAh bank daily or need USB-C output
specs: Folding fabric panel with grommets for hanging
verdict: The Anker PowerPort Solar 21W is the lighter, simpler folding panel for keeping one phone alive on the trail or through an outage. It gives up some margin to the 28W class in exchange for a slimmer pack.

**What 21W really means.** The rating describes the cells under ideal lab light. In good real-world sun, expect something like 8–13W through the USB ports, and Anker caps the pair at 3A combined, with 2.4A per port. Over 5 good sun hours that is about 40–65Wh, enough to fill a 10,000mAh bank like the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) (36Wh) with some left over.

**Use it to fill a bank.** Charging a phone straight off any panel works in clear sun but stops and restarts when clouds drift by. A power bank irons out the dips and stores the midday harvest for night. To fill a 20,000mAh bank every day, step up to the [BigBlue 28W](/gear/bigblue-28w-solar-charger/).

**Built to hang.** Anker lists SunPower cells, two USB-A ports with PowerIQ device detection, and a fold-flat fabric body with grommets for hanging from a pack, a tent or a balcony rail. Face it squarely at the sun and re-aim it every hour or two; that does more than any spec difference between panels in this class.

Owners like the light weight and steady output in clear sun. The main complaints are the lack of USB-C and the many Anker model names this panel has been sold under. It is the lightweight pick in our [best solar power bank](/best-solar-power-bank/) roundup; for a cheaper twin, see the [Nekteck 21W](/gear/nekteck-21w-solar-charger/).
pros: Slim and light enough to ride on a daypack

cons: USB-A only, with no USB-C output

faqs.q: Can the Anker PowerPort Solar 21W charge two phones at once?
faqs.a: Yes, in strong sun. It has two USB-A ports rated up to 2.4A each, but the pair shares 3A total, and real output drops whenever the sun weakens. With two devices connected, each charges more slowly. For the best results, charge one power bank during the day and share it at night.

faqs.q: Does the Anker PowerPort Solar 21W work through a window?
faqs.a: Poorly. Window glass and the angle through it cut output sharply, often to the point where a phone will not charge at all. Put the panel outside in direct sun, facing the sun squarely, and run a USB cable indoors if you need to. Hanging it from a balcony rail or tent works well.

name: Nekteck 21W Solar Charger
description: An inexpensive 21W folding USB panel with two USB-A ports; a sensible spare for a car or outage kit, paired with a charged 10,000mAh power bank.
quick: 21W folding USB panel, 2 USB-A ports. An inexpensive 21W folding USB panel with two USB-A ports; a sensible spare for a car or outage kit, paired with a charged 10,000mAh power bank.
bestFor: A low-cost solar charger for a car kit or emergency bag
skipIf: It will see weekly use on a pack, where a better-known brand is worth it
specs: Folding fabric panel with loops for hanging
verdict: The Nekteck 21W is a sensible, inexpensive solar charger for an emergency kit. It follows the same formula as the Anker 21W, with a fold-out fabric panel, two USB-A ports and loops for hanging, usually for less money.

**The physics are the same across the class.** A 21W rating describes ideal lab light. In good real-world sun, expect roughly 8–13W through the USB ports, or about 40–65Wh over 5 good sun hours. That fills a 10,000mAh (36Wh) bank, or puts about half a charge into a 20,000mAh bank like the [Anker 335](/gear/anker-335-power-bank-20000mah/).

**Build the kit around it.** Pack it with a charged 10,000mAh power bank and a short cable. During the day, charge the bank from the panel; at night, charge phones from the bank. With a few hours of decent sun, that keeps one or two phones going through a multi-day outage. It will not charge a laptop, since there is no USB-C Power Delivery.

**Where the savings come from.** Nekteck saves on brand depth and accessory polish, not watts, and it lists SunPower cells like the pricier panels. For a car kit that comes out twice a year, that is the right trade. If it will hang off a pack every weekend, the [Anker PowerPort Solar 21W](/gear/anker-powerport-solar-21w/) or [BigBlue 28W](/gear/bigblue-28w-solar-charger/) is worth the extra money.

Owners report it charges phones fine in direct sun and like the price. The main complaints are output that drops sharply in clouds, common to every panel this size, and the lack of USB-C. It is the budget pick in our [best solar power bank](/best-solar-power-bank/) roundup.

faqs.q: Is the Nekteck 21W good enough for an emergency kit?
faqs.a: Yes, if you pair it with a power bank. In direct sun it produces roughly 8–13W of real output, about 40–65Wh over a good day, which keeps one or two phones going through a long outage. It needs direct sun; on heavily overcast days it may barely charge. Store it with a charged 10,000mAh bank.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Nekteck 21W and the Anker PowerPort Solar 21W?
faqs.a: Mostly brand and price. Both are 21W fabric folders with two USB-A ports and SunPower cells, so they produce about the same energy. The Anker adds PowerIQ device detection and a longer track record; the Nekteck usually costs less. For an occasional-use emergency kit, the Nekteck is the better value.

name: BioLite SolarPanel 10+
description: A rigid 10W solar panel with a built-in 3,200mAh battery, kickstand and sundial; a tidy all-in-one charger for a solo hiker or a single phone in an outage kit.
quick: 10W panel with built-in 3,200mAh battery and kickstand. A rigid 10W solar panel with a built-in 3,200mAh battery, kickstand and sundial; a tidy all-in-one charger for a solo hiker or a single phone in an outage kit.
bestFor: Solo hikers who want a self-contained panel and battery in one unit
skipIf: You need to keep several phones charged, where a bigger panel and bank win
specs: Integrated kickstand and sundial for aiming
10W panel with built-in 3,200mAh battery and kickstand
verdict: The BioLite SolarPanel 10+ is the one all-in-one solar charger here with an honest balance of panel and battery. It is a small system, best for a solo hiker or a single phone in an outage kit.

**A real panel with a small buffer.** This is not a big battery with a token solar cell. It is a genuine 10W panel backed by a 3,200mAh battery, roughly 12Wh. The battery keeps power flowing to your phone when a cloud passes, so charging does not cut out, and it stores part of the afternoon harvest for later. Read [watt-hours](/glossary/watt-hours/) to see why 3,200mAh is less than one charge for most current phones.

**Aim it and leave it.** BioLite adds an integrated kickstand and a small sundial that shows when the panel faces the sun squarely, the easiest free gain in solar charging. In good sun, 10W of panel delivering a real 5–7W makes roughly 25–35Wh over 5 hours.

**Know the scale.** That is about two phone charges a day at best, delivered slowly. For a family, a 21W or 28W panel with a separate bank such as the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) gives more for similar money. For a backpacker who wants one rigid, self-contained unit, the 10+ is tidy and simple.

Owners like the kickstand, the sundial and the steady charging through passing clouds. The main complaints are the small battery and slow charging outside strong sun. It is the panel-with-battery pick in our [best solar power bank](/best-solar-power-bank/) roundup; for more output, see the [BigBlue 28W](/gear/bigblue-28w-solar-charger/).

faqs.a: Not from its battery alone. The built-in 3,200mAh battery holds roughly 12Wh, and after conversion losses that is less than one full charge for most current phones, which hold 12–19Wh. In strong sun, the panel keeps charging the phone directly, so a full day outside can add about two charges.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the BioLite SolarPanel 10+ and the BigBlue 28W?
faqs.a: Self-contained versus more output. The BioLite combines a 10W rigid panel, a small battery, a kickstand and a sundial in one unit. The BigBlue is a 28W fabric folder with three USB-A ports and no battery. The BigBlue harvests roughly two to three times as much energy, but it needs a separate power bank.

name: BLAVOR Solar Power Bank 10000mAh
description: A rugged 10,000mAh power bank with USB-C, a Qi wireless pad, a flashlight and a small solar cell; buy it for the battery and treat the solar cell as an emergency trickle.

skipIf: You expect to recharge it from the sun in a day

Rugged rubberized shell with built-in flashlight
10,000mAh bank, Qi wireless, USB-C, small built-in solar cell
verdict: The BLAVOR Solar Power Bank 10000mAh is a solid rugged power bank, and a fair buy if you think of the solar cell as an emergency trickle rather than the way you will charge it.

**Do the solar math.** A cell the size of a phone makes on the order of 1–2W in ideal sun. The battery holds about 37 [watt-hours](/glossary/watt-hours/). Even at 2W with no losses, that is over 18 hours of perfect sun, which in real life means several days on a dashboard or windowsill. Use the cell to win back a little charge when nothing else is available, and charge from the wall, a car or a folding panel the rest of the time.

**As a power bank, it does well.** You get USB-C and USB-A ports, a Qi wireless pad on top for phones that support it, and a built-in flashlight that earns its keep in a blackout. Wireless charging wastes more energy than a cable, so use a cable when the outage drags on. At 10,000mAh, expect about two charges for a typical phone.

**The better solar setup.** If solar charging matters to you, pair a plain bank with a separate folding panel. A [BigBlue 28W](/gear/bigblue-28w-solar-charger/) can fill a 10,000mAh bank in a few good sun hours, a job that takes this cell days.

Owners like the tough shell and the flashlight. The main complaints are how slowly the solar cell charges and the bank heating up when left in the sun. It is the built-in solar pick in our [best solar power bank](/best-solar-power-bank/) roundup; for a plain pocket bank, see the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/).

faqs.q: How long does the BLAVOR solar power bank take to charge in the sun?
faqs.a: Days, not hours. The built-in cell makes roughly 1–2W in ideal sun, and the battery holds about 37Wh, so a full solar charge needs 20 or more hours of direct, perfect sun. In practice that means several days. Charge it from USB-C or a folding panel, and treat the cell as a backup trickle.

faqs.q: Is it safe to leave the BLAVOR power bank in the sun to charge?
faqs.a: For short, supervised periods, yes, but heat is the enemy of lithium batteries. A dark power bank in direct sun, or on a car dashboard, can get hot enough to shorten battery life and slow charging. Avoid hot dashboards in summer, and move it to shade if it feels hot to the touch.

name: Anker 335 Power Bank (20,000mAh)
description: A plain 20,000mAh (74Wh) USB-C power bank with no solar cell; the battery half of the best solar setup, paired with any 21W–28W folding panel.
quick: 20,000mAh (74Wh) USB-C power bank, no solar cell. A plain 20,000mAh (74Wh) USB-C power bank with no solar cell; the battery half of the best solar setup, paired with any 21W–28W folding panel.
bestFor: Storing a folding panel’s daytime harvest to charge phones at night
skipIf: You need laptop-class USB-C output or a pocket-sized bank
specs: 20,000mAh USB-C power bank, no solar cell
verdict: The Anker 335 is the battery half of the best solar charging setup. It is a plain 20,000mAh power bank with no solar cell, and that is the point: paired with a 21W or 28W folding panel, it stores the midday harvest and charges your phone at night.

**What 74Wh buys you.** Anker rates it at 20,000mAh, about 74 [watt-hours](/glossary/watt-hours/). After roughly 20% conversion losses, about 59Wh reaches your devices, or three to four charges for most phones. That is a long weekend of normal use, or several days of careful use in an outage.

**Why a separate bank beats a built-in cell.** A solar cell built into a bank makes a watt or two. A folding panel such as the [BigBlue 28W](/gear/bigblue-28w-solar-charger/) makes 12–18W in good sun, so it can put 60–90Wh into this bank on a long clear day. On a typical day you add a third to a half, which still covers a family's phones. Charging the bank from the panel also avoids the start-stop charging phones do in passing clouds.

**Know its limits.** It has USB-C and USB-A ports and recharges over USB-C, but it is not a laptop-class bank. For laptops, step up to the [Anker 737](/gear/anker-737-power-bank/) with 140W USB-C. It is also heavier than a 10,000mAh bank, so it lives in a bag or drawer rather than a pocket.

Owners like the capacity for the price and Anker's reliability. The main complaint is slow charging compared with newer high-watt banks. It is the bank-to-pair pick in our [best solar power bank](/best-solar-power-bank/) roundup.

faqs.a: About one to two sunny days. The bank holds 74Wh, and a 21W panel delivers roughly 40–65Wh over a day of good sun after real-world losses. A 28W panel such as the BigBlue cuts that to about one long clear day. Clouds, low winter sun and poor aiming can double the time.

faqs.q: Can the Anker 335 charge a laptop?
faqs.a: Not well. It is designed for phones, tablets and small USB devices, not laptops that need 45W or more of USB-C Power Delivery. For laptops, choose a bank like the Anker 737, which delivers up to 140W over USB-C, or a bank or power station with an AC outlet.

name: Anker Prime Power Bank (27,650mAh, 250W)
description: A 27,650mAh (99.54Wh) power bank with 250W total output and 140W from one USB-C port; the most laptop power you can carry on a plane, with a live display.

bestFor: Keeping two laptops working through an outage or a long flight

specs: 250W total; up to 140W from one USB-C
verdict: The Anker Prime 27,650mAh is the most capable laptop power bank you can still carry onto a plane. It pushes capacity right to the airline limit and has the output to charge two laptops at once.

**As big as a power bank gets.** Anker rates it at 27,650mAh, or 99.54Wh, just under the 100Wh limit airlines allow without approval. After roughly 20% conversion losses, about 80Wh reaches your devices: five or more charges for most phones, or more than one full charge for a 70Wh laptop. See [watt-hours](/glossary/watt-hours/) for the math.

**250W is the headline.** Anker lists 250W of total output across two USB-C ports and one USB-A, with up to 140W from a single USB-C. That is enough to run a large laptop at full speed while also charging a tablet or a second laptop. In an outage where work does not stop, that matters more than any other spec.

**Where it sits next to the 737.** The [Anker 737](/gear/anker-737-power-bank/) holds 86.4Wh and tops out at 140W total. The Prime adds about 13Wh of capacity and far more total output for two devices at once. If you only charge one laptop and some phones, the 737 does the job for less. A smart display on the Prime shows remaining charge and live watts.

Owners praise the output and the display. The main complaints are the size and weight of a dense brick, and the premium price. Power banks must go in carry-on luggage, never in checked bags. Check your airline’s rules before international trips, since a few carriers set stricter limits of their own.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Anker Prime 27,650mAh and the Anker 737?
faqs.a: Capacity and total output. The Prime holds 99.54Wh versus 86.4Wh and delivers 250W across its ports, while the 737 tops out at 140W total. Both deliver up to 140W from a single USB-C port, so one laptop charges about as fast on either. Buy the Prime to charge two laptops at once.

name: Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC
description: A 94.7Wh power bank with a 100W AC outlet, 100W USB-C, Qi wireless and an 8mm solar input; for laptops with barrel chargers and small AC devices on the move.

bestFor: Laptops with barrel chargers and small AC devices away from an outlet
skipIf: You need to run anything over 100W, such as a fridge or a kettle
specs: AC outlet, 2 × USB-C PD (100W and 60W), 2 × USB-A, Qi wireless pad
None built in; 8mm input for Goal Zero Nomad panels
94.7Wh, 100W AC outlet, USB-C PD, Qi wireless
verdict: The Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC is a power bank with a real AC outlet. It is the bridge between a phone bank and a power station, for laptops with barrel chargers, camera batteries and other small AC devices.

**What 94.7Wh runs.** Goal Zero rates it at 25,600mAh, or 94.7 [watt-hours](/glossary/watt-hours/), under the 100Wh airline limit. Through the AC outlet, inverter losses of 15–20% leave about 75–80Wh. A 10W LED lamp runs for most of a night, and a 40W laptop for nearly two hours. The [power station runtime calculator](/tools/power-station-runtime-calculator/) does the math for your devices.

**The AC outlet is the point.** The outlet is rated at 100W, enough for laptop power bricks, camera chargers and small electronics, but not for a fridge, kettle or anything with a motor. Beside it are two USB-C PD ports (100W and 60W), two USB-A ports and a Qi wireless pad, so it charges five or six devices at once.

**Solar-ready.** An 8mm port takes Goal Zero's [Nomad 20](/gear/goal-zero-nomad-20/) and larger Nomad panels, and USB-C PD recharges it from the wall or a car. At about 2 lb, it is heavy for a pocket but light for anything with an outlet.

Owners like the AC outlet and the build quality. The main complaints are the price and the 100W limit, which rules out higher-draw gear. Compare it with the picks in our [best battery pack with AC outlet](/best-battery-pack-with-ac-outlet/) roundup; for more AC power, see a small station like the [Jackery Explorer 240 v2](/gear/jackery-explorer-240-v2/).
pros: Real AC outlet rated at 100W in a 2 lb power bank
USB-C PD at 100W and 60W, plus two USB-A ports
Qi wireless pad for compatible phones
8mm input for Goal Zero Nomad solar panels
94.7Wh, under the 100Wh airline limit
cons: 100W AC limit rules out motors and heating devices
Inverter losses leave about 75–80Wh through the AC outlet
Costs more than USB-only banks of similar capacity

faqs.q: Can the Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC run a CPAP?
faqs.a: For a few hours, without the humidifier. After inverter losses it delivers roughly 75–80Wh through the AC outlet. A CPAP drawing 30–40W without heated humidification would run about two hours. For a full night, use a dedicated CPAP battery or a power station of 300Wh or more, and check your machine’s actual draw first.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Sherpa 100AC and a power station?
faqs.a: Size and output. The Sherpa holds 94.7Wh with a 100W AC outlet and weighs about 2 lb. A small power station like the Jackery Explorer 240 v2 holds about 2.7 times the energy with a higher-watt outlet, but weighs several times as much. Pick the Sherpa for laptops and small electronics on the move.

name: Anker 733 Power Bank (GaNPrime PowerCore 65W)
description: A 10,000mAh power bank that doubles as a 65W wall charger with folding prongs; use it as your everyday charger and it is always full when the power goes out.
quick: 10,000mAh power bank that doubles as a 65W wall charger. A 10,000mAh power bank that doubles as a 65W wall charger with folding prongs; use it as your everyday charger and it is always full when the power goes out.
bestFor: People who forget to charge power banks and want one that is always full
skipIf: You need laptop-class capacity on battery
specs: Built-in folding AC plug or USB-C
GaN wall charger and power bank in one, folding prongs
verdict: The Anker 733 is a wall charger and a power bank in one, which makes it a smart bank for an outage kit. It sits plugged into the wall as your everyday charger, so it is already full when the power goes out.

**The always-charged advantage.** Most power banks fail in an outage for one reason: nobody charged them. The 733 has folding AC prongs and works as a 65W GaN wall charger when plugged in, topping itself up while it charges your phone and laptop. Pull it from the wall when the lights go out and it becomes a 10,000mAh battery.

**What 36Wh buys you.** At 10,000mAh, about 36 [watt-hours](/glossary/watt-hours/), expect roughly two phone charges after conversion losses. That makes it a pocket bank, not a laptop bank. Output drops from the 65W wall-charger figure when it runs on battery alone, so treat laptop charging on battery as a top-up.

**Ports for a desk.** Two USB-C ports and one USB-A let you charge three devices at once from the wall. On battery, plug in the device that matters most first, since every port draws from the same 36Wh.

Owners like having one less brick to pack and a bank that is always full. The main complaints are the small capacity for its size and the lower output on battery. For more capacity, pair it with the [Anker 737](/gear/anker-737-power-bank/), or see the picks in our [best portable chargers for power outages](/best-portable-chargers-for-power-outages/) roundup. The [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) holds the same energy in a smaller body.

Recharges itself whenever it is plugged in
Two USB-C ports and one USB-A
One device replaces a wall charger and a pocket bank
cons: Only 36Wh, about two phone charges

Bulkier than a plain 10,000mAh bank

faqs.q: Does the Anker 733 charge itself while it charges my phone?
faqs.a: Yes. Plugged into a wall outlet, it works as a 65W GaN charger for your devices and recharges its own 10,000mAh battery as well. That is its main advantage for outages: if you use it as your everyday charger, it is full when the power goes out, instead of sitting forgotten and flat in a drawer.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Anker 733 and the Anker PowerCore 10000?
faqs.a: The 733 doubles as a wall charger. Both hold 10,000mAh, about 36Wh, or two phone charges. The 733 adds folding AC prongs, 65W output from the wall and USB-C ports. The classic PowerCore 10000 is smaller, lighter and cheaper, with a single USB-A port. Pick the 733 if you tend to forget to charge banks.
